title: SVM margins and support vectors
summary: Derive the geometric margin, connect it to the hard-margin objective, and explain support vectors and hinge loss.

sections.title: Textbook depth · Geometry first
sections.body: For $f(x)=w^\top x+b$, the distance from $x$ to the separating hyperplane is $|w^\top x+b|/\lVert w\rVert_2$. Scaling $w$ and $b$ changes the score but not the boundary, so the optimization needs a scale convention before 'largest margin' has a precise meaning.

math.explanation: The numerator is the signed classifier score after multiplying by the label, so a correctly classified point has a positive value. Dividing by the normal-vector length converts that score into a geometric distance.
math.name: Signed geometric margin
math.purpose: Use it to convert a label-scaled classifier score into distance from the separating hyperplane.

sections.title: Textbook depth · Hard margin
sections.body: With labels in $\{-1,+1\}$, require $y_i(w^\top x_i+b)\ge 1$. The closest feasible points then have geometric margin $1/\lVert w\rVert_2$, so maximizing margin is equivalent to minimizing the norm under the constraints.

math.explanation: The constraint fixes the arbitrary scale by placing the closest correct points at score one. Once scale is fixed, a smaller norm means a wider geometric margin.

symbols.meaning: smooth objective equivalent to minimizing the norm

math.name: Hard-margin SVM objective
math.purpose: Use it when every training point is assumed separable and the goal is the widest feasible margin.

sections.title: Textbook depth · Support vectors and slack
sections.body: Support vectors are the observations with active constraints or non-zero dual multipliers; they determine the boundary in the dual representation. When perfect separation is unrealistic, slack variables and hinge loss allow violations while still penalizing them.

sections.title: Scope boundary
sections.body: This page is textbook depth. Treat the derivation as a worked mathematical extension and verify the current lecture sequence before calling every SVM detail examinable.

examples.title: Worked example: compute one geometric margin
steps: A point has $y(w^\top x+b)=2$ and $\lVert w\rVert_2=4$.
Divide the label-scaled score by the normal-vector length: $\frac{2}{4}$.
The signed geometric margin is $0.5$. A larger norm with the same score would reduce the geometric distance.
examples.answer: The margin is $0.5$; keep the label inside the numerator when using the signed form.

criticalQuestions.prompt: Why is the SVM scale convention necessary?
criticalQuestions.angle: Show what happens if $(w,b)$ is multiplied by a positive constant.
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: The boundary is unchanged but the raw scores change. Fixing the closest scores at one removes this arbitrary scale and makes the geometric margin comparable.

criticalQuestions.prompt: When is a hard-margin SVM the wrong model even if a separator exists?
criticalQuestions.angle: Consider noise, outliers, measurement error, and the cost of treating every point as perfectly separable.
criticalQuestions.modelAnswer: A separator can be created by an outlier or an overly flexible feature map. Soft margins and validation can produce a more robust boundary.
